opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there are a few reasons, and they compound on each other. The first is simply that the scaling still works. Every time we put more compute into training these models, with the right data and the right architectures, we keep seeing new capabilities emerge. We haven't hit a wall. There may be diminishing returns in some dimensions, but the returns are still very much worth it, so you'd be foolish not to keep pushing.

The second is that training is only half the story now. Increasingly, the interesting work happens at inference time: models that think, plan, search, and check their own reasoning before answering. That's very reminiscent of what we did with AlphaGo, where the neural network gave you intuition but the search on top gave you the real strength. Once you let systems think for longer, compute demand scales with how hard the problem is and how many people are using it. And if these systems become useful assistants for billions of people, running all day, that's an enormous amount of compute.

Third, and this is the part I'm most excited about, is science. If you want to simulate biology, design new materials, model a virtual cell, or work on fusion, those are effectively bottomless problems. There's always a more accurate simulation or a bigger search space. So I don't see a natural ceiling there.

And then of course we'll get more efficient. Algorithms improve, chips improve, and we'll squeeze a lot more out of each unit of compute. But historically, efficiency gains don't reduce total demand. They open up new uses. So my expectation is that, at least on the path to AGI and probably well beyond it, the appetite for compute keeps growing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses growing compute demand but does not identify data-center bandwidth as a constraint on distributing training compute.

r002.rationale: It says systems can think longer at inference time and compares search on top of a neural network to gaining strength, communicating that additional inference compute can improve capability.

r003.rationale: The response predicts more demand as assistants become useful to billions, but does not clearly say that improving AI capabilities will increase demand for AI systems.

r004.rationale: It says inference is increasingly important, but does not predict that inference will eventually account for more compute than training.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think there are a few reasons, and they compound. The first is just the scaling trend itself. We've seen, fairly consistently now for over a decade, that when you increase the amount of compute and data you put into these systems, you get predictable improvements in capability. There's no sign yet that that curve has flattened in a fundamental way. We may be seeing some diminishing returns on pure pre-training, but then new axes open up, like inference-time compute, where the model actually thinks longer about a hard problem, and that turns out to be another dimension you can scale.

The second reason is that the use cases are expanding. It's not just training one big model anymore. Once you have systems that are genuinely useful, people want to use them constantly, across every domain. And if you want agents that plan, that use tools, that run experiments in science, that's many, many more forward passes per task than a simple chat response. So demand on the inference side grows even faster than on the training side.

And then the third thing, which is the one I care most about, is science. If you look at something like AlphaFold, or what we're trying to do with materials, with fusion, with weather modelling, these are problems where you're effectively simulating very complex systems. Even with much more efficient algorithms, which we are also working hard on, the sheer breadth of problems worth attacking means compute remains the bottleneck for a long time.

I should say, I don't think it's only about brute force. Algorithmic efficiency has historically improved as fast as hardware has, maybe faster. We're very focused on that, because ultimately the brain runs on about twenty watts, so we know far more efficient approaches exist. But in the near term, if you have more compute, you can explore more ideas faster, and that itself accelerates finding the efficient algorithms. So the two go hand in hand.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention bandwidth between data centers or distributing training compute across locations.

r002.rationale: It says inference-time compute lets a model think longer about a hard problem and that this is another dimension to scale for capability gains.

r003.rationale: It connects increasingly useful systems and expanding use cases with people wanting to use them constantly, communicating that greater usefulness drives demand.

r004.rationale: It says inference demand grows even faster than training demand, suggesting inference will account for a larger share of compute over time.

astra-6.text:
I think there are several reasons. We’re still seeing gains from training larger models, but training is only one part of the picture. There’s also the compute you use when a system is actually solving a problem. For a difficult scientific question, you might want it to explore different hypotheses, check its reasoning, and spend more time searching before giving you an answer. That could take substantially more compute than a quick conversational response.

Then there’s scale of use. If these systems become useful to billions of people, and to scientists and businesses, the aggregate demand could be enormous—even as we make each individual operation more efficient.

So I don’t think it’s simply about making the next training run bigger. It’s also about how much thinking we want these systems to do, and how widely we use them.

r002.rationale: It says systems can spend more compute exploring hypotheses, checking reasoning, and searching longer to answer difficult questions, communicating that additional inference-time compute can improve performance.

r003.rationale: It predicts large aggregate demand if systems are widely used, but does not say that capability improvements will increase demand.

r004.rationale: It says training is only one part of compute demand, but does not predict that inference will eventually account for more compute than training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few reasons. One is that we’re still seeing substantial improvements as we scale these systems, and there’s a lot more we want them to be able to do—reason reliably, build models of the world, and help us solve difficult scientific problems.

But it’s not just about the compute you use to train a model. There’s also the compute it uses when you ask it a question. For a really hard problem, you might want the system to explore several possible solutions, check its work, perhaps run simulations. That could require much more computation than producing an immediate answer.

And then there’s demand. If these systems become useful to billions of people, and to scientists and businesses, the total amount of computation could grow enormously, even as we make each individual operation more efficient. So I think algorithmic efficiency and growing compute needs will happen together.

r001.rationale: The response discusses training and inference compute but does not identify data center bandwidth as a constraint on distributing training across locations.

r002.rationale: It says extra compute at inference can let a system explore possible solutions, check its work, and run simulations on hard problems, conveying greater problem-solving capability from more test-time compute.

r003.rationale: It links systems becoming useful to more people, scientists, and businesses with enormous growth in total compute demand.

r004.rationale: It says inference adds to training compute needs, but does not predict that inference will eventually account for more compute than training.
